title: Conflicting advice on whether it's safe to discharge a capacitor with a screwdriver
summary: Do not short a capacitor with a screwdriver. Identify the equipment and use its rated discharge and verification procedure.

blocks.title: Two confident answers, one missing question
blocks.body: A spark is not proof of safe discharge. Shorting with a screwdriver can cause an arc, tool damage, component failure and injury. Voltage, stored energy and the surrounding circuit matter; a story about one small capacitor does not establish a method for another.

columns.name: Anecdote
columns.detail: “It worked last time” describes an outcome, not a controlled current path or verified safe state.

columns.name: Engineering evidence
columns.detail: The equipment procedure specifies isolation, rated discharge provisions, wait time and verification for that circuit.

columns.name: Decision
columns.detail: Do not substitute a screwdriver or a generic resistor suggestion for that procedure.

blocks.heading: What you are actually dealing with
columns: What the number does not prove
rows: Low stored energy does not establish the condition of the surrounding circuit
Both high voltage and substantial stored energy require rated methods
Small capacitance is not permission to approach high voltage
Low voltage can still produce destructive short-circuit current
blocks.caption: Original calculations: E = ½CV². These are examples at specified actual voltages; a voltage rating is not a measurement of charge.

blocks.heading: What must be established first
items: Identify the equipment and its service procedure. If it is unknown, stop.
Use authorized isolation and rated discharge provisions; microwave ovens, CRT equipment and power converters are not beginner discharge projects.
A competent person verifies the required safe condition with suitable equipment and accounts for possible recharge or voltage recovery.
Do not use a meter lead as a shorting tool or assume a waiting period alone proves safety.

blocks.heading: Why the advice stays conflicting
blocks.body: For an ideal isolated RC circuit, voltage after five time constants is about 0.67% of its initial value. Starting at 2,100 V, that is still about 14 V; “under 1%” is not a universal safe condition. Real equipment adds stored energy, other sources, component ratings and recovery effects. Resistor pulse-energy and voltage ratings matter as well as resistance.

blocks.title: The cautious reader's takeaway
blocks.body: If you cannot establish isolation, ratings and a valid verification method, leave the equipment closed and seek qualified service. A resistor and insulated clips do not make every high-voltage job appropriate for a novice.

items.label: OSHA: control of hazardous energy
items.detail: Stored energy must be controlled and isolation verified; equipment-specific procedures govern.
